einzeiler: Tracing the evolution of Manhattan's Little Italy from an immigrant enclave to a theme…
kurzfassung: Manhattan's Little Italy has transformed from a densely populated late-19th-century immigrant enclave into a tourist-focused pocket neighborhood. The hosts explore the historical waves of Southern Italian immigration, the challenges of poverty and organized crime, and the lasting culinary traditions that survive today. Despite shrinking boundaries and modern gentrification, historic food shops and cultural celebrations like the Feast of San Gennaro endure.
stichpunkte: Little Italy has shrunk significantly over the decades, now spanning just a few blocks around Mulberry and Grand Streets.
The neighborhood's roots trace back to the massive wave of Southern Italian immigration between 1880 and 1920.
Early Italian immigrants faced severe poverty, dangerous day labor conditions, and exploitation by brokers known as padroni.
The area battled severe extortion and violence perpetrated by the Black Hand and later organized crime during Prohibition.
Legendary local institutions like Ferrara Bakery, Oliva Dairy, and Lombardi's Pizza were established during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
The annual Feast of San Gennaro, celebrating its centennial, remains a major cultural anchor for the neighborhood.
Post-World War II suburban migration and the expansion of neighboring Chinatown reduced the local Italian population.
Modern gentrification and rebranding efforts, such as the creation of Nolita, continue to threaten the historic district's boundaries.

clips.hook: Four million Italians arrived in the United States between 1880 and 1920.
clips.text: Ein Großteil der ankommenden Einwanderer bestand aus alleinstehenden Männern, die in den USA ihr Glück machen wollten, anstatt sofort dauerhaft umzusiedeln.

clips.hook: 75 percent of New York's day labor force was Italian by 1893.
clips.text: Italienische Arbeiter bildeten innerhalb eines einzigen Jahrzehnts den Großteil der tagelöhnerbasierten Arbeitskräfte in der Stadt.

clips.hook: One in twenty Italians in Five Points worked as an organ grinder.
clips.text: Straßenmusiker mit handgedrehten Orgeln und dressierten Affen gehörten im späten 19. Jahrhundert zum alltäglichen Straßenbild des Viertels.

clips.hook: New York had a dedicated Department of Combustibles due to frequent bombings.
clips.text: Wegen der extremen Dichte an Sprengstoffanschlägen und Erpressungen existierte in der Stadtverwaltung eine eigene Behörde für Brand- und Sprengmittel.

clips.hook: The last census shows zero Italian-born residents living in Little Italy.
clips.text: Inzwischen leben im historischen Viertel keine in Italien geborenen Menschen mehr, da die ursprüngliche Bevölkerung weitergezogen ist.

beschreibung:
How do vibrant New York City neighborhoods react to major changes to city life while retaining their historic character? For the next three weeks, we will present three neighborhood-history shows from the Bowery Boys podcast in a new light, exploring how these historic areas survive sudden changes in economic growth, housing needs and tourism. And listen to our prior shows on SoHo and Downtown Brooklyn.
Little Italy is the pocket-neighborhood reminder of the great wave of Italian immigration that came through New York City starting in the late 1870s. It was once a densely packed, vibrant district of pushcarts, cheese shops, barbershops, and organ griders, the home to thousands of new immigrants living in aging tenements.
The area still contains some of New York’s oldest continuously operating shops, from Ferrara Bakery to Di Palo’s. But the neighborhood also has a darker history, marked by Black Hand extortion plots and the enduring presence of organized crime.
Today’s Little Italy remains charming, though it continues to shrink, existing more as a tourist destination than a true Italian enclave. What does the future hold for this important landmark in American immigration history?
A version of this show was released in 2015—this newly re-edited and remastered version by Kieran Gannon. Watch an video version of this show, with a stroll through the neighborhood, on YouTube.
